newsitem.title: USA: Mideast summit delayed by working-level talks.
newsitem.headline: Mideast summit delayed by working-level talks.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Wednesday delayed a planned summit with leaders of Israel, the Palestinians and Jordan as deputies struggled with "serious differences" on how to restart the Middle East peace process.

"There are complicated, serious issues on the table. There are still serious differences between the delegations," spokesman Nicholas Burns said at the State Department, where Israelis and Palestinians haggled into the afternoon under the mediation of Secretary of State Warren Christopher."

Although there was no official confirmation of what the main sticking points were, Israeli officials accused the Palestinians of making unacceptable demands for an immediate Israeli withdrawal from the West Bank town of Hebron.
The Israelis said they were insisting on better security concessions on this, a central point of frictions in the region. The Palestinians had no immediate comment.

As the hour passed for a White House group summit that was supposed to cap the two-day crisis meeting, presidential spokesman Mike McCurry confirmed it had been postponed to give the deputies a chance to score a breakthrough.

Clinton called the summit after bloody clashes between Palestinians and Israelis last week threatened to scuttle the whole peace process. Hopes that tensions would be lowered were raised on Tuesday when Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat met alone for three hours in a White House residential library.
It was only the second direct meeting between the two leaders, previously known for ill-disguised mutual disdain.
But there apparently were no guarantees of tangible results at the emergency summit. "We are neither encouraged nor discouraged. We are determined to help the parties," McCurry told reporters.
He refused to rule out the possibility that the summit talks would continue beyond Wednesday, saying, "I have no idea how long they will last." But Burns seemed sceptical.
"I think our feeling is that we have a two-day summit scheduled and I believe we're still on track for that," he said at a separate State Department briefing.

The Israeli and Palestinian negotiators had worked nearly all night under lower-level U.S. mediation before continuing under Christopher's eye, and the U.S. summit hosts sought to put the most optimistic spin on this.
"There's a dynamic, fluid and improvisational character to these discussions," said Burns. "... We feel satisfied that they are engaged, they're working on the serious issues."
Netanyahu and Arafat restored a modicum of civility to Israeli-Palestinian relations with their long face-to-face talks over a lunch of chicken and couscous on Tuesday.
Gun battles and clashes in the West Bank and Gaza Strip last week took the lives of 57 Palestinians and 15 Israelis.
The original Wednesday schedule for the Washington talks foresaw Clinton hosting Netanyahu, Arafat and Jordan's King Hussein in the White House Blue Room late Wednesday morning.
That was to be followed by a working luncheon and public statements by the leaders summarizing the summit outcome.
But Israeli officials said Netanyahu was standing firm against U.S. pressure to set a date to complete a long-delayed pullback of troops from the West Bank city of Hebron.

Palestinians view Hebron, the last and most sensitive of the cities slated for handover under an agreement sealed at the White House one year ago, as a litmus test of Netanyahu's commitment to the peace deals he reluctantly inherited when he came to power at the head of a hardline government in June.

In Jerusalem, Palestinians stood in silent protest and Israelis marched in an annual religious pilgrimage as they tensely awaited the outcome of the summit. Apart from some stone throwing by youths in Hebron, protests in the West Bank and Gaza Strip were generally peaceful.

Last week's fighting was sparked by Israel's decision to open another entrance to a tourist tunnel alongside Jerusalem's Temple Mount, holy to Moslems and Jews. But it also reflected Arab frustrations at what they consider Israel's slow pace in pursuing peace accords.

Palestinians demand that Israel close the tunnel, carry out the pullback from Hebron -- home to 100,000 Arabs and 400 Jews -- and ease a closure barring Palestinians from jobs in Gaza and the West Bank.

Netanyahu wants guarantees for Israelis' security from Arab violence. He has accused Arafat of ordering his police to fire at Israelis with guns the peace deal provided. But a new opinion poll on Tuesday showed 80 percent of Israelis want him to make progress toward peace.
